For a pair (a, b), popcount(a OR b) + popcount(a AND b) = popcount(a) + popcount(b), since each bit position contributes exactly once across OR and AND. So a pair is excellent iff popcount(a) + popcount(b) ≥ k.

Pairs are ordered and duplicates of the same value count once per distinct value (num1 == num2 allowed if the value exists). Deduplicate nums, bucket distinct values by popcount c (at most ~30 buckets for values ≤ 1e9), then count ordered pairs of buckets with c1 + c2 ≥ k: for buckets a < b add 2·cnt[a]·cnt[b], for a == b add cnt[a]².

Example 1: distinct {1,2,3} with popcounts {1,1,2}; pairs summing ≥ 3: (1,3),(3,1),(2,3),(3,2),(3,3) → 5.
k: popcount(a OR b) + popcount(a AND b) = popcount(a) + popcount(b) — reduce the condition to a sum of popcounts.
Deduplicate first; only distinct values matter, and (v,v) is allowed.
Bucket by popcount (≤ 30 buckets) and combine bucket counts in O(30²).

a.i: Count distinct values per popcount, then double-loop over the ≤ 30 buckets adding ordered-pair counts whenever the popcounts sum to at least k.
s: Deduplicate nums; compute popcount of each distinct value into a Counter.
For each ordered bucket pair (a, b) with a + b ≥ k, add cnt[a]·cnt[b], halving off-diagonal contributions by iterating a ≤ b and multiplying by 2 when a < b.
a.t: O(n + B²) where B ≤ 30 is the number of distinct popcounts — deduplication and bucketing dominate.

w: The identity popcount(OR) + popcount(AND) = popcount(a) + popcount(b) is the entire problem; after seeing it, bucketing finishes in microseconds. Pitfalls: forgetting to deduplicate (inflating counts), treating pairs as unordered (they're ordered), and overflow (answer can reach ~1e10 — use 64-bit). Follow-up: count pairs with popcount sum exactly k, or handle 64-bit values (B grows to 64, still trivial).
